title: Handling large data volumes with PostgreSQL and YugabyteDB
author: Franck Pachot
body_html:
In the 100th episode of the "postgres.fm" podcast titled "To 100TB and Beyond!", Nikolay and Michael had guests to discuss the challenges and solutions of handling large data volumes with PostgreSQL. The episode explored how some companies addressed issues with large databases by building architecture, tools, and knowledge around PostgreSQL, whether it's self-managed or on Amazon RDS. YugabyteDB was created with similar goals and ideas, addressing PostgreSQL scalability limitations by adding built-in features to enable horizontal scaling, rather than adding complexity around multiple clusters. I'm sharing the notes I've taken when listening to the podcast and explaining what YugabyteDB changed to PostgreSQL to address these natively.

In this episode, Michael and Nikolay interviewed three database administrators from companies with more than 100 Terabytes in PostgreSQL:

  • Arka Ganguli. Notion operates a collaborative workspace that stores documents, wikis, and product management, in PostgreSQL. They employ a simple model (JSON, no foreign keys), with sharding being performed from the application using a common sharding key. The primary challenge they face is re-sharding.

  • Sammy Steele. Figma operates a real-time web-based SaaS that requires low latency and reliability. The model is complex, with no single sharding key, and queries can span multiple shards. To address this, they have developed a proxy that parses queries, splits them, routes them to the appropriate shards, and then aggregates the results.

  • Derk van Veen. Adyen processes financial transactions, requiring consistency, no data loss, and access to old data. To scale, they use partitioning and let partitions grow after reaching limits in the number of partitions. However, large partitions can cause issues when rebuilding indexes, blocking the XMIN horizon, increasing locks, and risking the infamous XID wraparound.

I have classified the problems mentioned, along with their solutions and the workarounds used in those companies to continue to run on PostgreSQL. I also explain how YugabyteDB avoids those problems thanks to built-in horizontal scalability. It is highly appreciated that the companies share publicly the problems they face because I encounter a lot of users at conferences who experience the same but feel that it's because of their lack of skills without realizing that those are general issues that are just more frequent in large companies.

Sharding

The need to shard urgently arrives when the vacuum starts to stall, with its sadly well-known consequences: bloat and transaction ID wraparound. Even if PostgreSQL can go far without scaling horizontally, doing it too late may put more pressure on the team and create fewer possibilities to do it because the migration will add more load on the source. However, doing it too early may constrain the data model as not all relational relationships are possible when sharding on top of it. To shard, Notion used double write with audit log and backfilling rather than logical replication, because logical replication didn't keep up with the non-sharded source.

YugabyteDB: Because sharding is at a lower level and transparent to the application, it doesn't restrict any SQL features. It is easier to shard early. Except for the small tables that will not grow and will be colocated, the tables are sharded on their primary key, and the indexes on their own key columns. It makes sense to start with only one tablet (the default when yb_use_hash_splitting_by_default = off) and it will be automatically split by the database when growing.

When using sharding on top of multiple databases, the level of effort required depends on the complexity of the model. For instance, Notion utilizes a simple sharding key, such as a tenant ID, and the application can straightforwardly handle queries for a single shard. If cross-shard query consistency is not necessary and a single shard key is used for all related tables, the complexity of implementation from the application side is minimal. Additionally, to avoid too much impact on the application, solutions like Citus can be employed when single-shard consistency (ACID, foreign keys) and local indexes meet the requirements. The challenge remains with re-sharding which is an operationally intensive process. Notion is thinking about moving its application to a cellular architecture.

YugabyteDB: Because tables and indexes are already split to tablets when the company is successful and the database grows, it is sufficient to start new nodes that attach to the YugabyteDB cluster and the database will automatically rebalance the tablet peers and raft leaders. The typical size of a tablet is 10 to 100GB so the rebalancing is granular. As soon as one is moved, some load is already reduced from the node it comes from. Depending on the size of the database, it may take hours to fully rebalance but this is a fully online operation where the application continues to run without stalling or getting errors.

When dealing with a complex data model, it's not always possible to use a single shard key for all tables. Some queries may need to involve multiple shards, and data may need to move between shards. This can make the application more complex. Figma has developed a custom stateless database proxy in Golang, featuring its own query layer that parses the query, builds an abstract syntax tree, splits queries according to a map of shard keys per table, sends queries to be executed on the shards, and aggregates the results. This approach resembles creating a database service, or at least its SQL processing engine, but is limited to their custom utilization. Figma mentioned that they borrowed CockroachDB's Postgres parser, so the limitation in SQL features is apparent. Additionally, the limitation in ACID features is the same as with all sharding solutions on top of PostgreSQL: cross-shard queries are not consistent (see Citus is not ACID but Eventually Consistent).

YugabyteDB: The same idea has driven the two-layer architecture of YugabyteDB, with a query layer that can scale because it is stateless and a storage layer that can scale because it distributes data storage, read and write operations, and ACID transactions. YugabyteDB uses the PostgreSQL code not only to provide all features but also to guarantee the same behavior at runtime. Re-writing a subset in a different language would have plenty of corner cases where datatypes and expressions are interpreted differently.

Partitioning

Partitioning is similar to sharding, but it occurs within a single PostgreSQL database. One key difference is that cross-partition queries are consistent due to the use of monolithic transaction control and a shared buffer pool. The datafiles, for tables and indexes, are physically separated based on a partitioning key. However, the other limitations remain. For example, global indexes are not possible, and all indexes must include the partition key, which restricts the possibilities for the primary key and unique constraints.

Partitioning offers the advantage of performing operations on full tables at the partition level, such as creating local indexes, analyzing optimizer statistics (no global statistics), and vacuuming. However, it's important to note that when dealing with very large partitions (e.g., 30TB for the largest one at Ayden), these operations need to be carefully managed to avoid freezing the XMIN horizon for extended periods, which can lead to bloat and XID wraparound issues. As a best practice, it's typically recommended to start partitioning when a table reaches 100GB in size. However, this would mean hundreds of partitions for a 10TB table, and this means several hundreds of tables and indexes for a simple query that has to read all partitions.

YugabyteDB: YugabyteDB also supports PostgreSQL declarative partitioning since it is based on PostgreSQL. In this approach, each partition is treated as a table, allowing the table and index partitions to benefit from storage-level automatic sharding. The declarative partitioning in YugabyteDB shares the same limitations as PostgreSQL in terms of SQL features, such as having local indexes only and requiring the partition key to be part of all primary key and unique constraints. Unlike PostgreSQL, YugabyteDB's declarative partitioning does not suffer from lock manager contention, vacuum, bloat, or wraparound problems. As automatic sharding has none of those limitations, with all secondary indexes being global and re-sharded on their own key, it is the right way to address scalability. Thanks to YugabyteDB distributed storage, declarative partitioning is typically unnecessary for scaling, but there are two use cases for it: data sovereignty and lifecycle management. In the former, partitions are assigned to specific regions based on the list of countries, while in the latter, data is partitioned by range to facilitate the dropping of old partitions rather than deleting large numbers of rows. Both cases do not need more than a handful of partitions and they can grow given that each partition is distributed.

In PostgreSQL, operations must be carefully planned to avoid problems. One example mentioned in the podcast is creating indexes on partitions one by one before creating the index at the parent level. This avoids running a long transaction that freezes the Xmin horizon while indexing all partitions. It is more difficult when dropping indexes because you cannot drop them per partition.

YugabyteDB:  the transactions are sequenced by the cluster Hybrid Logical Clock, which is based on the physical clock with an additional Lamport clock to make it monotonically increasing despite the possible clock skew between the servers. There will never be any wraparound and once a committed change has been recorded, it doesn't have to be modified later. The consequence of long transactions is, like in all Multi-Version Concurrency Control databases, the space amplification to keep the versions. YugabyteDB lets parameter the retention as it is preferable to cancel a runaway query rather than accumulating bloat.

Lock Manager, Custom and Generic plans

One problem that hits everybody when partitioning is the LockManager. During parsing, PostgreSQL has to lock the tables and indexes. The more partitions, the more indexes, and the more joins increase the CPU usage on the lock manager because it reaches the limits of fast path locks. In that sense, partitioning is not a way to scale as each additional partition increases the CPU usage. At Ayden, they decided to force the use of generic plans to spend less time in planning even if it increases the execution time. This may also involve stopping to add more partitions and letting the existing ones grow, with all the consequences mentioned above. At Figma, they experienced the same at the end of the vacuum when it analyzes the tables and invalidates the current generic plans, and then there's a storm of planning.

YugabyteDB: The database is designed to be scalable. Rather than locking the database objects that are shared by all connections, like with a central lock manager, YugabyteDB uses optimistic locking. The connections that cached the metadata from the catalog receive the change notification through heartbeats and can restart their read to see the changes.

Connection Pooling

PgBouncer was mentioned by all, as a connection pooler used in front of each shard. Connection pooling is mandatory for PostgreSQL applications because each connection to PostgreSQL is a process that allocates memory. As memory is not extensible, it is necessary to limit the number of connections. Another feature of pgBouncer is the ability to reduce downtime by draining the connections to zero for a short time using PAUSE/RESUME. This allows an asynchronous replica to catch up with the gaps and enables changing the pgBouncer configuration to switch over to the replica. This is used to reduce downtime for server maintenance, such as upgrades or re-sharding.

Some scalability issues with pgBouncer were mentioned, possibly because it is single-threaded, and considering pgCat instead.

YugabyteDB: The storage layer's auto-sharding feature provides elasticity and allows for more connections. Scaling out (adding new nodes) or scaling up (rolling restart with larger instances) is easy without stopping the application, so there is no need to pause/resume. 

However, it is always better to use a connection pool. YugabyteDB comes with a built-in connection manager that serves as a database-resident connection pool on each node, removing the need for a proxy between the application and the database. The YugabyteDB Connection Manager is based on Odyssey, which is multi-threaded and has been improved to support all SQL features. If it detects a session state that can't be shared in the physical connection, like prepared statements, session parameters, or session-wise temporary tables, the Connection Manager uses stickiness to maintain the state for the logical connection.

Upgrade

Upgrading PostgreSQL typically requires a few hours of downtime, and finding a suitable maintenance window can be challenging. This is why many companies continue to operate on older versions. It's even more complicated for SaaS and multi-tenancy setups because it's difficult to find one downtime window that works for all customers.

In the podcast, it was interesting to note that while some companies mention near-zero downtime solutions, they are still using PG13, at least for the largest databases. Notion has 90% on PG15 and this indicates that besides the volume and downtime, validating the application for a newer version is not an easy task, especially when the data model is complex. It was mentioned that backward compatibility is good in PostgreSQL when compared to MySQL, but it's still a challenge.

YugabyteDB: To facilitate upgrades and enable rolling upgrades, all new features include a GUC parameter to enable or disable them. Additionally, YugabyteDB installs pg_hint_plan by default, which helps to avoid or work around execution plan regressions.

Even though PostgreSQL is said to be nicely backward compatible, it seems that working with a very simple model is easier. It was noted that Ayden had to complete the upgrades within a maximum of 15 minutes. They have a near-zero downtime solution for PostgreSQL databases themselves, using logical replication, but mentioned that it's all the infrastructure around that takes time.

YugabyteDB: The primary reason for horizontal scalability is to be resilient to failures. This includes stopping a server in order to start it with a new version. You can perform rolling upgrades that are transparent to the application because a YugabyteDB cluster can run with nodes in two versions during rolling maintenance. The new features are activated only when all nodes are up with the new version.

One major concern was raised: the ability to revert to the previous version if something goes wrong. This could happen later, and reverting to the pre-upgrade system would result in a point-in-time recovery with potential data loss. Although Amazon RDS has a Blue-Green solution based on logical replication, it doesn't provide the option to roll back once the new environment is activated.

YugabyteDB: After a rolling upgrade, the database operates in a mode that is compatible with the previous version. This allows for a rolling rollback to the previous version if needed. Any new file formats introduced in the new version are enabled only after the application has been running for some time.

Logical Replication

Notion explained that logical replication, which is used to reduce downtime during migrations, cannot catch up to fill the gap after the initialization. They had to drop all indexes and recreate them afterward. In PostgreSQL logical replication, the system reads the physical changes from the Write-Ahead Log (WAL), reverses them to SQL statements, and applies them to the replica by going through the SQL layer. This process includes maintaining B-Tree indexes row by row and checking foreign key constraints, even if they were already validated on the source. It was also mentioned that Instacart performed the initialization with physical replication, which is faster, and then transformed it into a logical replica.

YugabyteDB: The replication process for tablets involves utilizing the internal API that connects the stateless SQL processing layer with the distributed storage (DocDB). When replicating the writes, it appears to the SQL layer as physical replication by distributing the key-value operations related to tables and indexes to the Raft groups. On the replica, it bypasses the SQL layer and writes directly to the tablet's WAL. From the point of view of the storage layer, it appears as a logical replication by applying key-value operations on physically different LSM trees. This enables cross-version replication (which is used during rolling upgrades). 

Read Replicas

PostgreSQL operates as a monolithic system, meaning that all consistent reads and writes must be processed from a single server. While it is feasible to read from replicas, it's only suitable for read-only workloads that can tolerate reading stale data, thereby not reflecting the most recent writes. The benefit of this approach is the ability to offload some activity to another server, which can prevent a slowdown that might affect availability. Additionally, Figma uses two read replicas to read data, in case one becomes unavailable. However, it's important to note that application redesign is necessary to isolate read-only services that can accept stale reads, which may not always be possible, particularly when dealing with sensitive data such as financial information. Notion also highlights that using an application cache, like Memcache, could make cache invalidation from the read replica challenging.

YugabyteDB: Because all nodes are active, the workload is automatically distributed. For read-only use cases that can accept a bounded staleness of a few seconds, it is possible to read from the Raft followers, which can reduce the latency when they are closer to the user. It is also possible to add read replicas that are similar but do not participate in the write quorum so that they do not impact the latency.

Fillfactor and WAL write amplification

In PostgreSQL, the Multi-Version Concurrency Control system creates a new version of the entire table row even if a single byte is updated. As a result, all indexes must be updated, even if the value hasn't changed, because the physical location has. To address this, it's recommended to allocate enough free space in blocks so that the new version of the row can fit into the same block as the previous version. In this case, the use of Heap-Only-Tuples can help avoid modifying all indexes, thereby reducing the number of page modifications and the associated Write-Ahead Logging (WAL). Achieving this optimization involves adjusting the FILLFACTOR, which can be challenging since it requires predicting how the existing tuples, as well as the new ones, will be updated. Additionally, when adding new indexes, regardless of this optimization, it means that more indexes need to be updated when inserting or deleting data and can defeat the purpose of Heap-Only-Tuples. On the other hand, with a FILLFACTOR too high, a lot of space is wasted, and that includes the pages in the PostgreSQL shared buffers as well as the Linux filesystem cache.

YugabyteDB: Because all table rows and index entries are stored in LSM trees organized by their key, the MVCC versions are always together, and rows are never addressed by their physical address. Therefore, there's no need to update the index entries. When a column is modified, only the new version for the column value is appended as a new version. In all cases, the WAL is minimal and doesn't need to log full pages. It has the same structure as the key-value API between the SQL layer and the Raft log that distributes the storage and transactions.

Throttling index creation

The podcast speakers mentioned that there is no way to slow down the creation of an index, and this could have an impact on IO throughput that is limited, especially in cloud environments. Some suggestions were made, such as decreasing the maintenance_work_mem and using only a single thread, but even these measures may still reach the limits of block storage. Additionally, slowing down the process could extend the XMIN horizon for too long, making it an unsuitable solution.

YugabyteDB: Index creation is done online by default, with concurrent backfilling that runs in parallel but is throttled on the servers. There is no XMIN horizon problem, so index creation can take a long time, if necessary, to save IO bandwidth for the application. It's also easy to overcome block storage limits by adding new nodes, and testing different storage service options can be done in a rolling fashion without downtime.

Foreign Keys

Referential integrity is a key feature of SQL databases as it ensures that data consistency will not be compromised even in the presence of race conditions. However, all the companies interviewed here had to limit their usage. When sharding on top of PostgreSQL databases, there is no cross-shard consistency, and foreign keys can only reference local tables, which works only if there's one sharding key for all use cases. It was mentioned that some companies create foreign key constraints without validation and manipulate the catalog to mark them as validated.

YugabyteDB: It is possible to choose not to enforce foreign key constraints when using YSQL, the PostgreSQL-compatible API. You can also use YCQL, the Cassandra-like API, which does not support joins or foreign keys. In both cases, the distributed storage is transactional, so you can benefit from ACID guarantees even when using a document model. With the PostgreSQL API, you can also store some data as documents using JSONB and GIN indexes within relational tables. As mentioned earlier, foreign keys do not impact replication, which operates on a level that has already been validated.

Support

Nikolay asked an important question about providing feedback to PostgreSQL hackers in order to enhance PostgreSQL for specific workloads. However, companies that use PostgreSQL in a managed service like Amazon RDS often engage with the support provided by the cloud service provider. I've noticed that when RDS PostgreSQL users seek assistance on PostgreSQL community channels, they are sometimes told that "RDS is not PostgreSQL" or "You have support, so don't ask the community". 

YugabyteDB: The same company, Yugabyte, is the main contributor to YugabyteDB and offers support and managed services. All feedback, whether from open-source users in the community channels or from users with commercial support, goes to the same product management team and helps to enhance the database for enterprise-level use. This also enables the company to prioritize the roadmap, develop features, and test them in preview or early adopter releases, even in production, with the validation of support engineers.

Conclusion

While all the techniques discussed in this podcast are fascinating, they require large teams to adapt the application and the infrastructure. Maintaining and evolving these techniques is a huge effort, and they are rarely compatible with a managed service or even for in-house management where teams can change, and new people have a hard time being operational on an over-engineered platform. For those unable to sustain such effort, it is better that those efforts are engineered within the database. That's why YugabyteDB has forked PostgreSQL to make it cloud-native, distributed, and resilient by itself.

YugabyteDB exposes one logical global database to the application, with no limitations on SQL features and ACID properties. The data distribution and replication are transparent to the application. This database is resilient to failure and allows online maintenance tasks such as scaling up and down, changing the storage, and upgrading the OS or the database for both minor and major upgrades.

There are many other issues that can occur with PostgreSQL on a large scale, such as those mentioned quickly by Nikolay: "wide-width locks, lock manager, multi-xact transactions, multi-xact IDs, and so on."

All of this doesn't apply to YugabyteDB because all architecture decisions have been made to be scalable. Not only are the table rows and index entries stored by key-value in the LSM tree, but also all transaction intents, without any per-block limits or memory structures to share between processes. Rather than monolithic shared structures that must be locked when accessed, the state of the database, data, or metadata is in the Raft logs, distributed, replicated, and consistent.

The beauty of PostgreSQL is its popularity and wide ecosystem. It allows database builders to enhance it in different ways, with tools or extensions, and to change the storage architecture while providing the same features.

This podcast is a valuable resource for information about operating PostgreSQL in large environments. I highly recommend listening to all 100 episodes. Congratulations to Nikolay and Michael for consistently producing this content every week.
